Name: Tony Twillie
Question: What does being tackled in American football feel like?
Answer: This is a question that can’t be easily answered because there is no “one size fits all” tackle. There are some tackles that are like when you’re a small kid and your large dog knocks you over. Pretty innocuous, no great shakes. There are some where you don’t get up. Most of them are in between those two, but understand that the range is vast. Most tackles hurt at least a little, whether it’s on the hit end or the hitting the turf end. But the adrenaline pumping through you from the game itself often numbs you to what’s really going on. You don’t really feel the pain. If you were a normal human and you were tackled like this, it would be a big deal. In a football game, you don’t feel it the same way. Plus a football player’s body is more conditioned to hits like this. They practice hitting, so they are more prepared for it. Plus, with the training done, your body is harder and can withstand the tackle better. Suffice it to say more times than not, it doesn’t feel good. But it doesn’t really hurt unless you fall awkwardly.

Question: What are some possible explanations for why so many NFL players have a low net worth despite making millions of dollars?
Answer: The definition and calculation of net worth is assets minus liabilities. Many pro athletes have lots of liabilities but few assets. First, let’s back up. The average NFL salary is just under $3 million, but we’ll say $3m for the sake of discussion. You’re in the top tax bracket so by the time all is done, you’re taking home just over $1.5 million. Now, that is OUTSTANDING money. But it’s not life altering money. If you’re 24 years old, you’re not going to live the rest of your life on $1.5 million dollars. And the NFL is not for long, so if you only make that money for 3 seasons, you’re not wealthy. You’re “rich”, and you can parlay that money into a lot more money, but you’re not wealthy enough to have and maintain a high net worth. Now, let’s say you’re a younger player in the league. You’re going to have cash, and you’re likely to put some money in savings. As for a car, that’s a nice today asset, but cars depreciate, so unless you bought an antique car, it’s not holding value for your net worth. You’re not likely out with your early earnings buying real estate. You may buy a home, but you’re going to have a mortgage likely, which is a liability, taking away from your net worth. Unless you paid cash for that car, you have an auto loan. You are lucky that you likely got a full scholarship so you don’t have any student loan debt. But often players take out personal loans early because they don’t have cash on hand, and that consumer debt is a liability. This is why players often have low net worths. They borrow against their future earnings so they have money, but not assets, and their liabilities take away from their net worth.

Question: Do people hate New Orleans Saints fans? Why or why not?
Answer: I’m a New Orleans Saints fan, so I’m answering from the inside out. Here’s what happens when an opposing fan comes to New Orleans. First, they are treated to a getaway in a truly unique city; one unlike any other in the US. It’s almost a Caribbean devil-may-care vibe. They can partake in the fun of the French Quarter or Frenchman Street, they will eat at some of the best restaurants in the country. They may visit a national museum dedicated to WWII. New Orleans is a perfect weekend city because it’s small enough that you can see and do a lot in just one weekend. You’ll head to the game on Sunday. You’ll be clowned with by people tailgating with loud music in nearby parking lots. If you clown back, they’ll laugh and likely invite you over for some jambalaya or BBQ. If it’s winter and it’s cold, they may even have gumbo. And if they do, trust me, it will be better than the gumbo in 90% of the restaurants in town. You’ll sit in the Superdome and unless you’re in a large group of loud, rowdy, raucous fans of your team, you’re likely to spark up a conversation with folks around you from here. They’ll ask where you’re from and how you’re enjoying the city. They’ll tell you were to go get great food postgame. And they might even invite you to come with them postgame to a few spots they’d like to hit for drinks. New Orleans doesn’t do pretension. We’re having a good time. You came here because you wanted to have a good time. That’s enough for us. This is the city where celebrities come to hide in plain sight. Our fans are loyal to the Saints and you’re not going to put them down. WE can (and will on occasion) talk bad about them, but you can’t. As long as you’re not coming in with guns blazing talking trash, you’re not going to be accosted by a Saints fan. Every year, I see at least one altercation in the stands, and it’s usually a fan - inebriated - who is in their team’s jersey and who has taken it upon themselves to tell Saints fans where they can go. And usually, it’s that fan who ends up going with NOPD “escorts”. To the contrary - I went to a game in Seattle and was just rudely harassed by several fans on the way to the stadium, in the stadium, and on the way from the stadium. It was a lot. I’ve also been to Miami and while most of the fans were very laid back, one guy kept riding me. He sat next to me, seeming to be looking for big reaction from me. As the Saints fell behind, he got more boisterous and obnoxious. When the Saints came from behind, I said nothing; I just kept looking at him with every TD we scored, until we went up by 2 scores and he got up and left. And when he did, the other fans around us were kind of thankful because they were embarrassed by him. And I’ve been to two Saints/Tampa Bay games in Tampa, but those were different because Tampa was a bad team at the time and their fans didn’t much show up for games. The first one I went to, Saints fans were nearly equal in number to Tampa fans. PLEASE come to New Orleans for your team’s game against the Saints.

Question: How in the world did the US Supreme Court decide that the US government does not have the right to ban bump stocks? Democrats, Republicans, Trump, the NRA, and more than 80% of all Americans supported banning bump stocks!
Answer: I don’t think the NRA’s “endorsement” of regulation of bump stocks was much more than an attempt to thwart further gun regulation. Kind of a thing where they say “we don’t want you messing with anything else, so we’ll give you this one”. It was a knee jerk reaction to the mass killing in Las Vegas in 2017. They knew they had little ground to stand on there. As for the Supreme Court decision, it’s only slightly quizzical, given the makeup of the court. But the scope of the question was narrow. The window they were looking through was small - does the bump stock in and of itself make a weapon automatic; meaning does the weapon itself change characteristics. And the answer to that is no. The bump stock is an individual object. It cannot on its own be considered automatic weaponry, despite it’s singular use. The bump stock uses a semi automatic weapon’s recoil to allow the gun to fired in rapid succession. What it doesn’t do is allow a single pull of the trigger to fire off multiple shots - the recoil of the bump stock bounces the weapon allowing multiple pulls in rapid succession. Yep, that’s it - the question that was asked of the Supreme Court was probably the wrong one, and they gave the only possible answer. I’d also be willing to bet the question posed to the Court was set up that way by the NRA. They would not want to make the bump stock manufacturers upset, and they knew how to work around their own words. So the decision of the SC, despite it’s ridiculousness, was the correct answer given the question asked and our definition of automatic weapons. The government can ban automatic weapons, but it can’t ban a device used to make a weapon automatic unless the specific function of that device is to make multiple shots fire rapidly with one pull of the trigger. It doesn’t matter that the reality is you only depress your finger one time and the bump stock does the rest, apparently.

Question: How does signing an incorrect scorecard lead to disqualification in golf tournaments?
Answer: Each day during a tournament when a round ends, you are to turn in your scorecard, signed by you - which is your affidavit saying that these numbers are true and accurate. That is still today, the only way a score is accepted. Despite all the technologies that exist, the bottom line is the score you turn in to the official scorer is your official score. So obviously, when you sign on a card that has a score you didn’t shoot, trouble could ensue. Now if you shot a 72 and sign and return a card that says 73 or more, you are not disqualified because you’ve penalized yourself a stroke or more. It’s only when you turn in a scorecard for a number lower than what you shot that there is an issue. When you return a scorecard for a number lower than your actual score, it’s as though you are cheating the system and the field. Even if you’re not intentionally trying to cheat, it projects as such, and in reality it is an aggression to the field. To protect the field, you have to disqualify that person. In golf, it’s one of the more egregious errors there is.

Question: Who is the golfer with the most major wins but has not won any PGA Tour events?
Answer: Well, the majors are co-opted by each major world tour, so if you win a major, you have by definition won a PGA Tour event. They count as wins on each of the two major tours - the US PGA Tour, and the DP Tour in Europe. So when you win the US Open, that win counts on the DP Tour as well. My guess is that everyone who has won more than one major has won at least a singular other tour event. There are a few guys like Shaun Micheel whose only PGA Tour win was his PGA Championship. He did win events on the Nike Tour and the Asian Tour as well. I’m sure there are a few others with one major win and no other wins. I couldn’t find anyone with more than one major who only won those majors and nothing else.

Question: In the NFL, is there a correlation between preseason record and regular season record?
Answer: I really don’t think much can be inferred by preseason records; moreso today than ever. In the past when teams played 4 preseason games, it was common for starters to play up to the first half of the 3rd preseason game, then maybe one series in the final game. There was a move to make sure you had enough on field game situation reps so that you’re not walking into week one never having thrown to your receivers, taken a handoff from your QB, or blocking alongside your teammates. Today, none of that exists. You may or may not see your starting QB take preseason game snaps. You may or may not see the starting RB play. It’s now frowned upon due to the risk of injury. In practice, even the ones against other teams, they have controlled scrimmages where QB’s cannot be hit and the tackling is less than aggressive. In preseason, those things don’t exist, so they often pull the starters. It’s why the NFL sucks and is so unpredictable in the first 2–3 weeks of the season, and why there are so many injuries early on. But I digress… Because we see so few starters, we can’t correlate any success or failure with the regular season. We see the starters a little and then a lot of the second teamers. So we can kind of know what might happen if a starter gets hurt, but we don’t see enough of what we’ll see in the regular season to make a difference. The only thing you can really take from watching preseason is the crispness of passes, the decision making of QBs, the burst from a RB, the route running and hands of the WR, does the offensive lineman consistently beat their man, does the defensive lineman consistently beat their man, can the LBs stay in position and tackle, and can the DB’s cover. That’s a lot, but remember, you’re basing that on just a small handful of plays by the first teamers on either side of the ball.

Question: What does a one-and-a-half gap defensive front look like?
Answer: Here is a good look at a gap and a half front. The nose tackle is playing a zero technique, head up on the center. He’s responsible for either A gap. The defensive ends in this play (3–4 defense) are playing a 4i technique - they are lined up on the inside shoulder of the offensive tackles. They have responsibility for their B gaps, but they are squeezing down towards the center, so they are basically also giving aid to the A gap, creating a gap and a half - their B gap, plus assisting the A gap. The OLBs do a similar job, playing the C gap, but spying the B gap as well. This is a great run stuffing defensive call - you take away the A and B gaps and force the runner to bounce outside, where you have a LB or safety waiting.

Question: Founded in 1988, which team is the original Charlotte Hornets now, the Pelicans or the Hornets?

When the Bobcats formed, they were formed as an expansion team in the league. At that time, all the Hornets team records were in New Orleans. In 2014, the New Orleans team changed their name to the Pelicans and the Hornets retook their name. As part of the deal, the Pelicans were treated as a pseudo-expansion team. The Hornets were restored all their team records up to 2002, and then they merged those records with the Bobcats records, and now they are Hornets/Bobcats/Hornets records. However, the Pelicans retain those records for the Hornets from their time in New Orleans, so everything that happened in New Orleans stays in New Orleans, but what happened before New Orleans in 2002 goes back to Charlotte. While I like the Pelicans name well enough, can we please get the Jazz to give up a name that has never - ever - fit them in Utah?

Question: What is the highest paying sport for athletes, excluding endorsements, and why? Is there a significant difference in pay between the NBA, MLB, NFL, NHL, and PGA Tour golfers?
Answer: If we’re talking averages, the NBA has the highest average salaries, at $10.82 (just behind Formula One racers). Baseball follows but far behind at around $5 million. Hockey is next at $3.5 million and surprisingly to many, the NFL would bring up the rear in average salary at $2.8 million a year. So yes, there is a significant difference between the average NBA player, and the average NFL player. Why? Well, despite the NFL dwarfing the total revenue of the NBA (and every other major sport on earth), there are far more people to pay in the NFL. NFL rosters are 53 players, as well as a host of coaches and support personnel. The NBA roster is only 15 players with fewer support personnel. MLB has a 26 man roster, and the NHL 23. As for the PGA Tour, it’s not as much a “league” as a collection of individual contractors under one umbrella. It functions far different from the other major sports - you don’t have to play every week, your pay is based completely on production, you only get paid the top money if you win. It’s got more in common with auto racing than the big 4–5 sports where they play in leagues. The PGA Tour average for 2023 was $2.36 million a year. That’s only earnings. And while that’s an average, that is good enough for 81st place on the money list. Sounds really great considering 241 golfers made at least one paycheck last season. And it sounds like the average is skewed towards the top of the list. But that finish would have left you out of the season ending money in the FedEx Cup race. However, you would be in the Top 125 and retain your card for another season.

Question: It does seem to be the case that blacks are naturally dominant in sporting activities that demand physique, mental fortitude and stamina. Examples are athletics, boxing and basketball. What accounts for this phenomenon?
Answer: I think since there have been less than 80 black NHL players throughout history, that those who play hockey would like a word with you on blacks dominating sports requiring physique, mental fortitude, and stamina… Athletic dominance is created by a complex melange of factors; not the least of which is a ton of practice. There are certain traits of a population that may assist in athletic endeavors - people from certain areas of the world may have genetically inherited traits that allow for certain abilities to be more easily gained. Others have socio-economic factors that may lead to a perspective in which working harder at a sport could provide advantages for a person. In addition with the socio-economic factors, being able to afford to play certain sports is a factor. Environmental factors play a role as well - Scandinavians are tremendous at outdoor winter sports - is it because they’re white? No one would say that. It’s because of where they live. As well, if we talk about genetic predisposition, then shouldn’t it logically follow that Irish people make great police officers, or Jewish people are logically going to be the best comedians since there are historically an abundance of both groups in those professions? We don’t think of those things that way, so why would we think of sports as such? It shows the fact that there are a lot of reasons things happen the way they do that ae beyond race (which is a social construct anyway…).

Question: How do professional golfers earn money if they don't win tournaments but make cuts during them?
Answer: Each tournament has a prize purse. That is all the monies available to the players who make the cut. You play Thursday and Friday, basically for free. If you don’t make the cut, you don’t get paid for the week (the US Open paid every participant who didn’t make the cut $10k, except for the amateurs who couldn’t receive that money). If you make the cut, you get a percentage of the purse, dependent on your finish. The winner in the regular events gets 18% of the total purse. Second place gets 10%. It goes on down to the last place, which gets 0.215% of the prize money. The breakdown is different for majors I think.

Question: Can you play NFL football at a height around 5′5″ and make good money from it? Think of the guy is very strong and fast to take on with the big guys on the team.

Name: Tony Twillie
Question: Why isn’t Troy Aikman considered the greatest 90s quarterback despite winning 3 super bowls?
Answer: Because of his numbers. Championship wins don’t always equal top level individual greatness. You asked the same question of Terry Bradshaw and the answer is exactly the same. It’s great to win Super Bowls. But those wins don’t necessarily mean you were the best QB of your day. Aikman was never an All-Pro. He made the Pro Bowl a bunch, but that only means he was a top 3–5 QB (or that better QB’s didn’t want to play…). Only once did he throw for more than 20 TDs, and he has 141 interceptions to his 165 TDs; not outstanding. Only once was he in consideration for the league MVP, and even that was only a 5th place finish for him. For his career, the people whose careers his most resembled were guys like Jim Kelly, Kenny Stabler, and Terry Bradshaw. All very nice QBs, all Hall of Famers, but none the best of their day. I’d have Kelly in front of Aikman for better in the 1990s, not to mention Steve Young, Brett Favre, and without question John Elway.

Question: What is the reason for the Saints having a high number of home games?

Question: Which tight end is better: the one who is great at blocking but not as good at receiving, or the one who is great at receiving but not as good at blocking?
Answer: The answer is yes… maybe… OK, the real answer is it depends on the offense. If you have an offense like Kansas City’s, you’re not looking as much for Travis Kelce to block - he’s a possession receiver. He can block - he’s a middle of the pack blocker, not killing in blocking assignments. But he’s catching passes. If you’re looking for a more in-line TE, you’re looking more at a guys like a Dalton Schulz or a Dawson Knox. They’re going to catch passes, but you’re looking for them to be very adept in blocking as well. Then, you have the unicorn. George Kittle is an outstanding blocker and an outstanding pass catcher. If you could have anyone, you’d want him. And maybe Mark Andrews. In most of today’s offenses with a strong passing attack, you’ll sacrifice a small amount of blocking for a guy who can catch 50–60 passes a season and get you 5–8 TDs.
